messages.subject: Re: plotmath for xlab()
messages.body_plain:
Hi:

Here are some possibilities:

d <- data.frame(x = 1, y = 1)

# (1)

ggplot(d, aes(x, y)) + geom_point() +

 xlab(expression(paste("red blood cell"%*%10^6,"/",mu, "L")))

although I might prefer cell to be plural :) The reason the original %*% didn't work is because the operator needs
both a left and right argument, and only the left one was given. The text string 'red blood cell' provides the needed left argument.

# (2) Another possibility (my preference):

ggplot(d, aes(x, y)) + geom_point() +

 xlab(expression(paste("red blood cells (",10^6, "/",mu, "L)")))

# (3) My initial stab at this was to use phantom, which works if its argument is an empty string, and contains the multiplication sign:

ggplot(d, aes(x, y)) + geom_point() +

 xlab(expression(paste("red blood cell (", phantom()%*%10^6,")/",mu, "L")))

Hopefully, one or more of these work for you...

Dennis

Vikram

messages.subject: Re: scale_colour_grey and name
messages.body_plain:
> The issue here is that scale_grey works on a sequential (discrete)
> scale as opposed to a continuous one.  So when it gets a continuous
> variable, it errors just like scale_shape would. (Which turns out to
> be a bad example because, in a bizarre turn of events, scale_shape
> works with continuous variables.  Try running qplot(1:10, 1:10, shape
> = rnorm(10)) .)

Yes, this is a long-standing bug that I need to fix :(

> I always thought that the grey scale was a kind of
> simplified wrapper for scale_gradient(low = 'black', high = 'white');
> is there a reason why it forces a discrete scale?

Because it's not a short cut for scale_gradient - it's a more like a
specialised version of gradient for discrete variables (when they are
actually ordered)

Hadley

Hi,

ggsave saves ggGrob object, not graphic device.
if you modify something outside ggplot2 and want to save it,
then you need use dev.copy, pdf, png, etc, depending on the device.

In your case, simply,

png(filename)

messages.subject_clean: Using a different scale for "background" tiles
messages.body_plain:
Hi:

One option is to use scale_alpha() on the tile instead of color, which would open up the color aesthetic for the points. It reverses the color shading (0 is close to white, 1 to black), but that shouldn't be a big deal. Here's my tweak; hopefully you can build on it. The second example is a toy to show how to manually coordinate shapes with fill colors.

create.fisherplot <- function(dat.fun, fisher.beta=1) {
    fisher <- expand.grid(x=seq(from=0, to=1, length=100), y=seq(from=0, to=1, length=100))
    fisher$z <- (1 + fisher.beta^2) * fisher$x * fisher$y / (fisher.beta^2 * fisher$x + fisher$y)
    fisher$z[fisher$x == 0 & fisher$y == 0] <- 0

    p <- ggplot(fisher, aes(x=x, y=y)) +
         geom_tile(mapping=aes(alpha=z)) + theme_bw() +      # add theme_bw()
         scale_alpha(name="Fisher", to = c(0.1, 1.0)) +             # replace color gradient with alpha
         stat_contour(mapping=aes(z=z), bins=5, colour="red") +
         geom_point(data=dat.fun, mapping=aes(x=precision, y=recall, colour=type, shape=type), size=4) +
         scale_x_continuous('Precision') +
         scale_y_continuous('Recall') +
         scale_color_brewer() +
         coord_equal(ratio=1)
    return(p)
}

print(create.fisherplot(dat))

# Toy example to illustrate manual definition of shapes and fill colors
df <- data.frame(gp = factor(rep(LETTERS[1:10], each = 2)),
                  x = rep(1:10, 2),
                  y = rpois(20, 5))

ggplot(df, aes(x, y, shape = gp)) + geom_point(aes(fill = gp), size = 3) +
  scale_shape_manual('Group', values = c(0, 1, 2, 5, 4, 22, 21, 24, 23, 8)) +
  scale_fill_manual('Group', values = c('A' = 'red', 'B' = 'blue', 'C' = 'green',

messages.subject: Re: Error in quantile plot
messages.body_plain:
Hi:

With a little reading between the lines on the help page, this appears to work:

data(Chem97, package = 'mlmRev')

p <- ggplot(Chem97, aes(sample = gcsescore))
p + stat_qq() + facet_wrap( ~ score) + ylab('gcsescore')

The problem with your code is that you tried to use ppoints(100), but
> table(Chem97$score)

   0    2    4    6    8   10
3688 3627 4619 5739 6668 6681

and that's why you got the error message - your attempt at defining y used a fixed number of ppoints() but there was inequality in the sample sizes in each score subgroup, all of which were not equal to 100. Using geom_point() with my above code doesn't work either because there is no 'y' defined. Since Hadley mentioned on the stat_qq() help page that qplot/ggplot was 'smart' enough to do the right thing, I trusted his word and voila :)

HTH,
Dennis

Hi, try this:

 scale_fill_continuous(low="black", high="red") +

 scale_alpha( breaks=c(0,1), labels=c('invalid','valid'), limits=c(-2,1) ) +
 opts(panel.grid.minor=theme_blank())
gg.wave

messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I have issues with a simple histogram.  I'm plotting a count variable (cfc) as a function of destination (dstroi) and condition (cond).  The output in Quartz looks fine, but whenever I save the plot (pdf, cairo_pdf, ggsave, it doesn't matter), it looks weird.  Here's two examples:

http://dl.dropbox.com/u/6281903/good.png
http://dl.dropbox.com/u/6281903/badandugly.pdf

And here's the code:

ggplot(subset(imca.CRI, srcroi%in%c(5:8) & dstroi%in%c(1:7))) +
  geom_histogram(stat="identity", aes(x=dstroi, y=cfc, fill=cond)) +
  xlab("Zielwort") + ylab("Anzahl Fixationen") +
  facet_wrap(~cond) + theme_pm() + opts(legend.position="none") +
  scale_fill_manual(values=c("#73d216","#cc0000")) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks=1:7,
                     labels=c("A","verb-te","B","weil","er","Pr+1","Pr+2"))

ggsave(file="cri.pdf", width=7, height=3.5)

I excluded everything unnecessary and the problem persists.  The data frame is quite large with 1 380 000 rows, but I tried to plot a subset from only five subjects and that yielded the same result.  Finally, I tried geom_bar and geom_histogram, it doesn't make a difference.  Does anybody have an idea how to solve this?

Best,
Paul

messages.body_plain:
Hi Ista:

To allay your concerns, plotmatrix() can handle factors:  :)

library(ggplot2)
str(OrchardSprays)
plotmatrix(OrchardSprays)

The problem with PY's data set is that  cu.summary contains missing values in both Reliability (ordered factor) and Mileage (numeric):
> sapply(cu.summary, function(x) sum(is.na <http://is.na>(x)))
      Price     Country Reliability     Mileage        Type
          0           0          32          57           0

I tried making Reliability an ordered factor with NA as a valid level, but still got warning messages re missing values with mileage, so it appears, at least on the surface, to be an NA handling problem. In cu.summary, we have the following table of the number of missing values per line:

library(rpart)
table(apply(cu.summary, 1, function(x) sum(is.na <http://is.na>(x))))

 0  1  2
49 47 21

i.e., 21 observations have NA values for both Reliability and Mileage, 47 observations have one NA and 49 have no NAs.

>From the help page of plotmatrix, Hadley's warning was quite direct:

plotmatrix {ggplot2}R Documentation
Code to create a scatterplot matrix (experimental)
Description

Crude experimental scatterplot matrix

Fortunately, there are a number of useful scatterplot matrix functions in R, which one can find through

library(sos)
findFn('scatterplot matrix')

if one needs an immediate solution. To investigate missing values in particular, package VIM has a couple of neat little functions.

Dennis

messages.subject: Re: Striped bars in histogram/bar plot
messages.body_plain:
Hi:

This works on my system:

df <- data.frame(gp = factor(rep(c('Kongruent', 'Inkongruent'), each = 1000)),
                 Zielwort = sample(c('A', 'verb-te', 'B', 'weil', 'er', 'Pr+1', 'Pr+2'),
                               2000, replace = TRUE,
                               prob = c(0.05, 0.075, 0.075, rep(0.2, 4))))
df$Zielwort <- factor(df$Zielwort, levels = c('A', 'verb-te', 'B', 'weil', 'er', 'Pr+1', 'Pr+2'))
df$gp <- factor(df$gp, levels = c('Kongruent', 'Inkongruent'))
g <- ggplot(df, aes(x = Zielwort))
g + geom_bar(aes(fill = gp)) + facet_wrap(~ gp, nrow = 1) + theme_bw() +
    scale_fill_manual(breaks = levels(df$gp), values = c('green','red')) +
    opts(legend.position = 'none') + opts(panel.border = theme_blank()) +
    opts(axis.ticks = theme_blank()) + ylab('Anzahl Fixationen')
ggsave('zeilbars.pdf', height = 5, width = 7)

(BTW, this is a bar chart, not a histogram - your Zielwort values are categorical, not numeric. Replaying this by summarizing df into a frequency table for Zielwort by each level of gp,

ddfrq <- ddply(df, .(gp), summarise, freq = tabulate(Zielwort))
ddfrq$Zielwort <- factor(rep(levels(df$Zielwort), 2),
                         levels = c('A', 'verb-te', 'B', 'weil', 'er', 'Pr+1', 'Pr+2'))
h <- ggplot(ddfrq, aes(x = Zielwort, y = freq))
h + geom_bar(aes(fill = gp), stat = 'identity') + theme_bw() +
    facet_wrap(~ gp, nrow = 1) +
    scale_fill_manual(breaks = levels(ddfrq$gp), values = c('green','red')) +
    opts(legend.position = 'none') + opts(panel.border = theme_blank()) +
    opts(axis.ticks = theme_blank()) + ylab('Anzahl Fixationen')
ggsave('zeilbars2.pdf', height = 5, width = 7)

The second of these is attached; both worked, both are identical. If this doesn't work on your system, you should check the versions of R, ggplot2 and plyr against mine. I didn't do this test in a fresh session, which is why a bunch of unrelated packages are loaded below.

HTH,
Dennis

messages.subject: bug-like behavior from geom_smooth()
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I've noticed some bug-like behavior in simple usage of geom_smooth() where it seems that the choice of xlim and ylim can affect the computation of smoothed means.  A simple example is given below:

library(ggplot2)
set.seed(2)
N <- 100
x <- runif(N)
y <- 0.2 * x + rnorm(N)
qplot(x,y) + geom_smooth(method="loess",lwd=2)
quartz() ## change quartz() to x11(), etc. as needed
qplot(x,y,ylim=c(min(y),max(y)) + c(-1,1) * 0.3 * (max(y)-min(y))) + geom_smooth(method="loess",lwd=2) ## expanding range doesn't change curve shape
quartz()
qplot(x,y,ylim=c(min(y),max(y)) + c(1,-1) * 0.3 * (max(y)-min(y))) + geom_smooth(method="loess",lwd=2) ## shrinking range and cutting off points does change curve shape
quartz()
qplot(x,y, xlim=c(min(x),max(x)) + c(1,-1) * 0.3 * (max(x)-min(x))) + geom_smooth(method="loess",lwd=2)  ## same with xlim -- note that we're now below y=0 at x=0.6

It looks to me like the values of the dataset that don't fall in the given xlim and ylim ranges are simply omitted when the smoothed means are computed.

Best

Roger

--

Roger Levy                      Email: rl...@ucsd.edu
Assistant Professor             Phone: 858-534-7219
Department of Linguistics       Fax:   858-534-4789
UC San Diego                    Web:   http://idiom.ucsd.edu/~rlevy

messages.subject: Re: bug-like behavior from geom_smooth()
messages.body_plain:
Hi Roger,

You are exactly correct that points falling outside the limits are
excluded from the smooth calculation; however, this is expected
behavior.  ggplot2 is more than just a way to blot some ink on a page,
it is an entire way of relating data to a visualization.   xlim and
ylim do not "zoom" in or out when used in qplot, they change your
data, and because of the integrated nature of ggplot2, that (the
change in data) changes your graph.

If you want to zoom, use coord_cartesian().  Here is an example:

require(ggplot2)
set.seed(2)
dat <- data.frame(x = runif(100), y = rnorm(100))
qplot(x, y, data = dat) + geom_smooth()
dev.new <http://dev.new>() # start new default device
qplot(x, y, data = dat) + geom_smooth() +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(.2, .6))

HTH,

Josh

Here is a short function that would help you achieve this. It is a
quick hack and there might be more elegant ways to do this with lesser
lines of code. Let me know if this works.

foo <- function(x){

  require(ggplot2);
  df1 = data.frame(x = density(x)$x, y = density(x)$y);
  df2 = data.frame(t(boxplot.stats(x)$stats));
  names(df2) = c('xmin', 'fq', 'med', 'tq', 'xmax');
  df  = data.frame(df1, df2);

  p0  = ggplot(df, aes(x, y)) +
        geom_line() +
        geom_errorbarh(aes(x = 0, xmin = xmin, xmax = xmax, y = max(df
$y)/2), height = 0.05) +
        geom_linerange(aes(x = med, ymin = 0, ymax = y)) +
        geom_area(subset = .(x > df$fq[1] & x < df$tq[1]), fill =
'green', alpha = 0.5)

}

prove fruitful.

messages.body_plain:
Hi:

The main problem with RV's function was that the plot was never printed. However, grabbing the data from density() and boxplot.stats() was inspired - nice job. I rewrote the plot part of the function and added several intermediate statistics to make some of the segment locations a little more precise. I hope this works...

kdeBxp <- function(x){

 require(ggplot2)
 # Data frame for generating the kernel density

 df1 = data.frame(x = density(x)$x, y = density(x)$y)

 # Data frame for holding the boxplot statistics

 df2 = data.frame(t(boxplot.stats(x)$stats))
 names(df2) = c('xmin', 'fq', 'med', 'tq', 'xmax')

 df2$ymx <- max(df1$y)     # maximum density value
 df2$ymid <- df2$ymx/2     # midpoint of the densities

# Find observed point closest to median and its corresponding y value in df1,
# put in new data frame df3 - this is used to get the vertical segment
  u <- which.min(abs(df1$x - median(df1$x)))
  df3 <- data.frame(x = df1$x[u], y = df1$y[u])

# Determine endpoints of the horizontal whiskers:
df2$iqr <- with(df2, tq - fq)
df2$wmin <- with(df2, max(xmin, fq - 1.5 * iqr))
df2$wmax <- with(df2, min(xmax, tq + 1.5 * iqr))

 p0 <- ggplot() + geom_line(data = df1, aes(x, y), size = 1, color = 'blue') +
    # vertical segment at the median
             geom_segment(data = df3, aes(x = x, y = y, xend = x, yend = 0)) +
    # left and right segments, respectively
             geom_segment(data = df2, aes(x = wmin, y = ymid,
                              xend = fq, yend = ymid)) +
             geom_segment(data = df2, aes(x = tq, y = ymid,
                              xend = wmax, yend = ymid)) +
    # vertical whiskers - reset 0.02 to change height
             geom_segment(data = df2, aes(x = xmin, y = ymid - 0.02,
                                          xend = xmin, yend = ymid + 0.02)) +
             geom_segment(data = df2, aes(x = xmax, y = ymid - 0.02,
                                          xend = xmax, yend = ymid + 0.02)) +
    # filled 'box'
             geom_ribbon(data = subset(df1, x >= df2$fq & x <= df2$tq),

Hi:

After reflecting on this (about five seconds after I sent it off...oy), the x-value in df3 should be the median of x rather than the x-value that is closest to the median, so the 'more correct' version would be

kdeBxp <- function(x){
 require(ggplot2)
 # Data frame for generating the kernel density
 df1 = data.frame(x = density(x)$x, y = density(x)$y)
 # Data frame for holding the boxplot statistics
 df2 = data.frame(t(boxplot.stats(x)$stats))
 names(df2) = c('xmin', 'fq', 'med', 'tq', 'xmax')
 df2$ymx <- max(df1$y)     # maximum density value
 df2$ymid <- df2$ymx/2     # midpoint of the densities

# Find observed point closest to median and its corresponding y value in df1,
# put in new data frame df3 - this is used to get the vertical segment
  u <- which.min(abs(df1$x - median(df1$x)))

  df3 <- data.frame(x = median(df1$x), y = df1$y[u])     ## <<== change is here

# Determine endpoints of the horizontal whiskers:
df2$iqr <- with(df2, tq - fq)
df2$wmin <- with(df2, max(xmin, fq - 1.5 * iqr))
df2$wmax <- with(df2, min(xmax, tq + 1.5 * iqr))

 p0 <- ggplot() + geom_line(data = df1, aes(x, y), size = 1, color = 'blue') +
    # vertical segment at the median
             geom_segment(data = df3, aes(x = x, y = y, xend = x, yend = 0)) +
    # left and right segments, respectively
             geom_segment(data = df2, aes(x = wmin, y = ymid,
                              xend = fq, yend = ymid)) +
             geom_segment(data = df2, aes(x = tq, y = ymid,
                              xend = wmax, yend = ymid)) +
    # vertical whiskers - reset 0.02 to change height
             geom_segment(data = df2, aes(x = xmin, y = ymid - 0.02,
                                          xend = xmin, yend = ymid + 0.02)) +
             geom_segment(data = df2, aes(x = xmax, y = ymid - 0.02,
                                          xend = xmax, yend = ymid + 0.02)) +
    # filled 'box'
             geom_ribbon(data = subset(df1, x >= df2$fq & x <= df2$tq),

    # bells and whistles
             theme_bw() + opts(panel.grid.major = theme_blank(),
                               panel.grid.minor = theme_blank()) +
             geom_hline(aes(yintercept = 0), color = 'gray90')

 print(p0)
 invisible()

}

messages.subject: Re: Is it possible in ggplot2 to create a combined boxplot and kernel density estimate
messages.subject_clean: Is it possible in ggplot2 to create a combined boxplot and kernel density estimate
messages.body_plain:
This is one way, but one can fiddle with the details to get what one wants...

df <- data.frame(gp = 1, x = rnorm(100))
g <- ggplot(df)
p1 <- g + geom_density(aes(x = x), fill = 'green', alpha = 0.4) + theme_bw() +
          xlim(-3, 3) + xlab("")
# Some of the options used below are to ensure that the scale of x is the same
# in both the density plot and the box plot
p2 <- g + geom_boxplot(aes(x = gp, y = x), fill = 'orange') + theme_bw() + ylim(-3, 3)  +
        opts(axis.text.y = theme_text(colour = 'white'),
             axis.title.y = theme_text(colour = 'white'),
             panel.grid.major = theme_blank(),
             panel.grid.minor = theme_blank(),
             axis.ticks = theme_blank(),
             panel.border = theme_blank(),
             axis.ticks = theme_blank(),
             axis.text.x = theme_blank()) +
        coord_flip()

grid.newpage()
pushViewport(viewport(layout = grid.layout(20, 1)))

vplayout <- function(x, y) viewport(layout.pos.row = x, layout.pos.col = y)
print(p1, vp = vplayout(1:18, 1))
print(p2, vp = vplayout(18:20, 1))

Some comments:
(1) I needed to create a phony grouping variable to get ggplot2 to plot a single boxplot,
     which is why gp has one value in the input data frame df.
(2) I used a large number of rows in the layout argument of viewport to have finer
     control over placement of the two graphs. There are other, probably better ways to go about this.
(3) If the code from grid.newpage() down is not familiar, it is taken out of p. 154 of Hadley's
     book. Another viable option would be to use the gridExtra package for this task.

Dennis

Sorry, I'm confused, which plot did you want help with?  The second seems to be working for you, no?  So you want to adapt the syntax you used for the second (which is 'pre-summarized' data) for the first (which is not summarized/counted)?

Having said that I think you will figure it out from

http://had.co.nz/ggplot2/geom_bar.html

the trick, if I understand you right, is realizing that with geom_bar you don't need a 'y' variable in the aes (ie ggplot2 generates the count).

ggplot(data, aes(Date)) + geom_bar() + scale_x_date(format = "%b")

With that in place probably the more interesting question is: how do I organize the count by month/week, ie set the binwidth appropriately.  That I'm not as sure about.  I had thought that it would be expressed in seconds, but messing around with

data <- data.frame( date = seq(Sys.Date(), len=100, by="1 day")[sample(100, 50)], price = runif(50) )

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I've build and am in the process of submitting a bioconductor  R
package.
I use ggplot2 to plot heatmaps. I was asked to only import the
functions used
with importFrom (...). I'm struggling with this as, if I import all
the functions used,
there still appears to be other variables/objects declared elsewhere
that I'm unsure
how to include. Any help what be appreciated.

Regards,
Ed

The code for the heatmaps:
p <- ggplot(all.m, aes(variable, GeneNames)) +
      geom_tile(aes(fill = value),colour = "white") +
      scale_fill_gradient(low = "white",     high = "steelblue",
limits = c(0,1)) +
      opts(title = "Network Uncertainty", axis.ticks = theme_blank(),
axis.text.x = theme_text(angle = 30, hjust = 1)) +
      labs(x = "",y="") +
      scale_x_discrete(expand = c(0, 0)) +
      scale_y_discrete(expand = c(0, 0)) +
      facet_grid( Same ~ ProbType, scales = "free")

The import:
importFrom(ggplot2, ggplot.data.frame, aes, facet_grid, geom_tile,
ggplot, labs, opts,
           scale_fill_gradient, scale_x_discrete, scale_y_discrete,
           theme_blank, theme_text)

messages.subject: plotCI() with ggplot2
messages.body_plain:
Hello

Currently, I plot some coefficients with some intervals using
function "plotCI()" (package "gplots") using the following code:

(m1 <- matrix(0:5, nrow=2, byrow=T, dimnames=list(c("v1", "v2"),
   c("lo", "m", "hi"))))
m2 <- m1 + 1
library(gplots)
plotCI(
   x=1:length(m1[, 1]),
   pch="",
   xlab="v1/v2",
   xlim=c(1-.2, length(m1[, 1])+.2),
   ylim=c(-.1, 7.1), yaxp=c(0, 7, 7),
   ylab="Coefficients and intervals",
   xaxt="n"
)
plotCI(
   x=1:length(m1[, 1])-.1, y=m1[, 2], li=m1[, 1], ui=m1[, 3],
   pt.bg <http://pt.bg>="white", cex=1, lty=1, type="o", gap=0,
   add=T
)
plotCI(
   x=1:length(m2[, 1])+.1, y=m2[, 2], li=m2[, 1], ui=m2[, 3],
   pch=10, pt.bg <http://pt.bg>="white", cex=1, lty=1, type="o", gap=0,
   add=T
)
axis(1, at=1:length(m1[, 1]), labels=NA)
text(1:length(m1[, 1]), -.2, c("v1", "v2"), cex=1, xpd=T,
   adj=.5, srt=0)
abline(h=seq(0, 7, 1), col=gray(.7), lty="dotted", lwd=.85)
legend(1.9, 7.1,
   legend=c(".7", ".5"),
   title="Condition:",
   cex=.8
)

I like to produce this plot with package "ggplot2", but I have
just discovered it and don't know where to start. It would be
great if somebody could give me a starting point with code for
that particular task.

Thanks, *S*

--
Sascha Vieweg, sasch...@gmail.com

messages.subject: ggplot replacements for rms plots
messages.body_plain:
Harrell's plots within the rms package in general, and his bplot
(heatmap) function in particular generates elegant plots. However, I'd
like a bit more control over them then I can currently achieve within
bplot, so I'd like to do them within ggplot2.  I've got some code to do
faceted plots where there is just one continuous predictor, (e.g. time)
graphed against the continuous probability of the event, but... it is
the heat maps that have me stumped.

messages.subject: Re: Is it possible in ggplot2 to create a combined boxplot and kernel density estimate
messages.subject_clean: Is it possible in ggplot2 to create a combined boxplot and kernel density estimate
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

There's currently a danger in this approach, which is that the two x
axes may not be well aligned. Consider this,

p1 = p1 + ylab("verrrrrrrrrrrrrrrrrrrrrry long axis title") +
opts(axis.title.y=theme_text())

grid.newpage()
pushViewport(viewport(layout = grid.layout(20, 1)))

vplayout <- function(x, y) viewport(layout.pos.row = x, layout.pos.col = y)
print(p1, vp = vplayout(1:18, 1))
print(p2, vp = vplayout(18:20, 1))

If possible, facetting would be the best option. Other than that one would want,

- to calculate the width of the y axis label and of the optional
legend (see align.plots() in ggExtra)

or perhaps more easily

- to add a phantom() y axis label for the second graph

HTH,

baptiste

messages.subject: Re: Is it possible in ggplot2 to create a combined boxplot and kernel density estimate
messages.subject_clean: Is it possible in ggplot2 to create a combined boxplot and kernel density estimate
messages.body_plain:
I agree, Baptiste; if you look at the first two opts of the boxplot p2, I didn't get rid of the text or axis labels on what ended up being the y-axis of the rotated box plot - I simply 'painted' them white to match the background color. Getting rid of them would have distorted the scales on the two panels. Another concern would have been if the value of the grouping variable were different from the order of magnitude of the input vector - e.g., 1 for the group and 10xy for the values of the input vector - that would misalign the scales as well. The user would have to 'know' to substitute a value for the grouping variable in the box plot that was the same order of magnitude as the maximum response, or at least that of the largest label in the main plot.  My purpose was to show that it *could* be done, but I wouldn't write up what I did as a 'ready for production' function for the reasons you mentioned as well as the above. Dealing with where to put the x-axis labels was another headache...

A function to create a density/histogram + boxplot could overcome some of these issues - e.g., one could hard code the titles, to check the order of magnitude of the input vector and generate the grouping variable value accordingly, but these patches highlight the central problem - a more automatic way is needed to ensure that the horizontal scale of the two graphs align properly when rendered on the graphics device. In this situation, I'd be more comfortable writing such a function in base or grid graphics, since one would then have more control over the placement of the two graphics in question and could perform tests on each to ensure that both plots have the same horizontal scale.

Thanks for the appropriate warning...
Dennis

Hi,

The boxes plotted by the following code are very narrow. If I'm not
mistaken, I think that it is because to neighboring x locations are
too close to each other, and the width of the boxes is smaller than
the closest distance between two neighboring positions. I'm wondering
if there is a way to make the boxplot wider, even if there are
overlaps between boxes.

library(ggplot2)
dframe=data.frame(
    x=do.call(
        c
        , lapply(
            0:10
            , function(i) {rep(i*1000,10)}
            )
        )
    , y=do.call(
        c
        , lapply(
            0:10
            , function(i) {rnorm(10,i)}
            )
        )
    )
dframe=rbind(
    dframe
    , data.frame(
        x=rep(-1,10)
        , y= rnorm(10,-1)
        )
    )
qplot(x,y,data=dframe,geom='boxplot', group=round(x))

--

Peng

messages.subject_clean: Too narrow boxplot when two positions are close to each other (using group parameter)
messages.body_plain:
Hi:

Clearly, this is a pathological example:

with(dframe, table(x))
x
   -1     0  1000  2000  3000  4000  5000  6000  7000  8000  9000 10000
   10    10    10    10    10    10    10    10    10    10    10    10

Compare the following:

# (1) May as well use geom_linerange...
ggplot(dframe, aes(x, y)) + geom_point() + geom_boxplot(aes(group = x))
# (2) Still very narrow
ggplot(dframe, aes(x, y)) + geom_point() + geom_boxplot(aes(group = x), width = 100)
Warning message:
position_dodge requires non-overlapping x intervals
# (3) A bit wider...
ggplot(dframe, aes(x, y)) + geom_point() + geom_boxplot(aes(group = x), width = 300)
Warning message:
position_dodge requires non-overlapping x intervals
# (4) Remove the values at x = -1:
ggplot(subset(dframe, x >= 0), aes(x, y)) + geom_point() + geom_boxplot(aes(group = x))

Dennis

messages.subject: per cent on axis without using formatter
messages.subject_clean: per cent on axis without using formatter
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I would like to plot percentages of behaviour. To do so I used the formatter function that I found on Hadley’s website and in the archive of the ggplot group. The thing I don’t understand is if I have stat = "identity" anyway why does ggplot plot proportions instead of the numbers when I remove the formatter? Can anyone help me in getting rid of the % signs next to the numbers please? I would prefer to have it only once in the axis label. (The reason why I prefer % and not “proportion of ..” is because [%] uses less text.)

I attached a reproducible example below and also I attached it as an R-script. Besides, I attached the PDF of a preliminary version of the graph. Any general suggestions are of course welcome.

Many thanks and best wishes,

Martin

p.s.: One minor question: Does anybody know how to adjust the gap between lines of text when using “\n”?

p.p.s.: Another minor question: If you look at the name of scale_y_continuous you notice that I have added several space characters in order to roughly have both lines centred. Is there a better way of doing it? I’m sure this is not the correct way but without the space characters the second line is anywhere but not in the centre.

REPRODUCIBLE EXAMPLE:

library(proto)

library(grid)

library(plyr)

library(reshape)

library(digest)

library(ggplot2)

# setwd("C:\\Users\\mhk\\Documents\\nur.fueR\\melipona project\\graphs\\")

df1 <- data.frame(variable = rep(c("queenless\n", "queenright\n", "queenless\nelected", "queenless\nkilled"), each = 5),

       value = rep(c("walk/rest", "run", "attacked", "hide", "antennate"), 4),

       percent = c(22.45446970, 2.01348485, 31.97083333, 43.48484848, 0.07689394,

             10.16621279, 4.94666667, 42.14618421, 41.41775253, 1.32357855,

             30.16625000, 0.28750000, 3.07625000, 66.43000000, 0.04041667,

             21.89256989, 2.13607258, 34.17805645, 41.71469355, 0.07909946))

df1$variable.ord <- factor(df1$variable, levels = c("queenless\nelected", "queenless\nkilled", "queenless\n", "queenright\n"), ordered = T)

attach(df1)

ggplot(df1, aes(x = variable.ord, y = as.numeric(percent), fill = value)) +

       geom_bar(stat = "identity", position = "fill") +

       coord_flip() +

       scale_y_continuous(name = "queens' behaviour during first hour \n after introduction [%]         ", formatter = "percent") +

       scale_x_discrete(name = "colony state and queens elected or killed") +

       opts(axis.text.x = theme_text(size = 10, vjust = 0.9),

             axis.text.y = theme_text(size = 10, hjust = 0.52, angle = 90)) +

       opts(axis.title.x = theme_text(size = 11, vjust = -0.25, hjust = 0.71),

             axis.title.y = theme_text(size = 11, hjust = 0.8, vjust = 0.24, angle = 90)) +

       opts(legend.direction = "horizontal", legend.position = c(0.51, 0.97), legend.text = theme_text(size = 10),

             legend.title = theme_blank(), legend.background = theme_rect(colour = 0), legend.key = theme_rect(colour = 0),

             legend.key.size = unit(c(0.6, 0.6), "lines")) +

       opts(plot.margin = unit(c(1.5, 0.3, 0.4, 0.3), "lines")) +

       scale_fill_grey()

ggsave("plot.a.2.pdf", width = 90/25.4, height = 90/25.4, family = "Times")

messages.subject: connect means of boxplots with factor x
messages.subject_clean: connect means of boxplots with factor x
messages.body_plain:
Hi group,

Is there an easy way to render a line connecting the means of boxplots when the x-axis is a factor? I've looked into using stat_summary, but nothing seems to work when the x-axis is a factor - does it violate some sort of standard to include a line?

Anyway, here's an example - I'm simply trying to show with a connecting line the comparison between the distribution for factor level x and that of factor level y.

tst<-data.frame(a=rnorm(1000),b=c(rep("x",50),rep("y",50)))

ggplot(tst,aes(b,a))+geom_boxplot()

Thanks very much.

Adam Loveland

messages.subject: Specify variable as dataframe[index]?
messages.body_plain:
It seems to me that supplying variables in ggplot2 functions requires
specifying the actual variable name in the working data frame.  Is it
possible to specify the column index instead of the name?

For example, instead of using 'aes(y=Column2)', where "Column2" is the
name of the variable in the second column of the working data frame, I
would instead like to use something like 'aes(y=MyDataFrame[2])'.

Can it be done?  I get an error when I run code like the above.

Many thanks,
Mauricio

messages.subject: boxplot and colour
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I'm trying to plot a boxplot with colour depending on z. But it seems
that qplot don't show different colors. Does anybody know how to show
different color in a boxplot?

library(ggplot2)
dframe=data.frame(
   x=do.call(
       c
       , lapply(
           0:10
           , function(i) {rep(i*1000,10)}
           )
       )
   , y=do.call(
       c
       , lapply(
           0:10
           , function(i) {rnorm(10,i)}
           )
       )
   , z=sample(1:3,11*10, replace=T)
   )
qplot(x,y,data=dframe,geom='boxplot', colour=z, group=round(x))

--
Regards,
Peng

> Hi,

> I'm trying to plot a boxplot with colour depending on z. But it seems

That doesn't make any sense. Each boxplot summarizes data with
different levels on z. Take the first one:

        x           y z
1       0 -0.60559500 2
2       0  2.02828698 1
3       0 -2.92175858 2

7       0  0.16006550 1
8       0 -0.23953187 2
9       0  0.34809024 2
10      0  1.40467198 1

Now tell me, what color should this boxplot be?

You could do something like this:

qplot(x,y,data=dframe,geom=c('boxplot', 'point'), colour=z, group=round(x))

but as originally formulated the graphic does not work.

Best,
Ista

messages.subject: Re: wavelet transform plot
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I got the same vertical lines.
And when I changed the size of window, sometimes the lines eliminated and sometimes they appeared at different location.
If you specified colour in aes, then the unexpected lines never appears.

So, my inspection is that this is because of a kind of rounding problem of floating point numerics.
Generally, it is not easy to fix this problem.

Currently, this may be the best:

# convert date to numeric

wave.frame$time2 <-  as.numeric(format.Date(wave.frame$time, "%Y"))

gg.wave <- ggplot( wave.frame ) +

geom_tile( aes(x=time2, y=period, fill=power, alpha=coi)) +

 geom_contour( aes(x=time2, y=period, z=signif), color='white', breaks=siglvl ) +

 scale_fill_continuous(low="black", high="red") +

 scale_y_continuous( name='Period ( years )', trans="RevLog2") +

 scale_alpha( breaks=c(0,1), labels=c('invalid','valid'), limits=c(-2,1) ) +

 opts(panel.grid.minor=theme_blank())

--
Kohske Takahashi <takahash...@gmail.com>

Research Center for Advanced Science and Technology,
The University of  Tokyo, Japan.

Brandon

thanks for you help, koshke! it's now looking like what I want.

posix and tile dont seem to play well. in retrospect, i guess this should be obvious.  your suggestion works for yearly data, but a tad of extra trickery is necessary for more frequent data. instead of doing it the way you suggested, i opted to retain POSIXct while was being more careful with my POSIXct definitions (down to the second). This also solved the problem with a simple function (I'll paste that code at the end).

for curiosity sake and backing up a bit, should I expect to always define transformers in the global environment?

much appreciated,

James

## name: evenPOSIXct
## purpose: to make an evenly spaced POSIXct timeseries.

## ts - either:
##              a year.fraction timeseries *with potential gaps*
##              (e.g. c(1980.0, 1980.25, 1980.75, 1981.0) )
##      OR when used with origin and dY:
##              the length of an origin+dY generated timseries.
## origin, dY - must be supplied together
##      origin is a single year.fraction
##      dY - is the fraction of a year of the timestep.
## tz - the timezone for POSIXct class, set to default GMT
##      instead of the

evenPOSIXct <- function( ts , origin=NULL, dY=NULL, tz='GMT' ) {

  nts <- length(ts)
  if (nts==1) {
    if (missing(origin) | missing(dY))
      warning('Both origin and dY required for scalar first argument', immediate.=TRUE)
    ts <- origin + ( (0:(ts-1))*dY )
    nts <- length(ts)
  }

  y <- floor(ts) ; f <- ts-y  ## y.f

  ## now need to get the number of seconds in each year
  nsec=as.numeric(as.POSIXct(strptime(paste('01/01',y+1,sep='/'),format='%d/%m/%Y'),tz=tz)) -
        as.numeric(as.POSIXct(strptime(paste('01/01',y,sep='/'),format='%d/%m/%Y'),tz=tz))

  invisible(as.POSIXct(strptime(paste('01/01',y,sep='/'),
                       format='%d/%m/%Y'),tz=tz) + (nsec * f))

}

Hi Martin,

On Fri, Mar 11, 2011 at 7:01 AM, martin_kaercher
<martin_...@yahoo.de> wrote:
> Dear Ista,
>
> Thanks a lot for your help and sorry for my beginner’s questions.
> Position stack solved the problem. I could then also remove the
> formatter which I only used to actually have the percent instead of
> proportions on the axis.

Glad to hear you got it working the way you want.

 The trouble is that I have a lot of work
> apart from R and I don’t have the time to use it more often which is
> why I seem to forget the bascis :-( plus I’m still an R beginner.
> Thanks also for the advice on the line height. That’s a very useful
> detail that further improved the graph. Only one thing I did not
> understand: What exactly do you mean with “Don't mess with the hjust
> setting in opts(axis.title.x. You seem to be going out of your way to
> make things difficult. Try starting with the default theme options and
> only adjust the ones you need.” How else can I adjust the position of
> the axis label? How would you do it without using hjust and vjust if I
> don’t want to use grid.text? In my view graphs look nicer if axis
> labels are centered and this is very often not the case, at least
> after saving it as a PDF.

Well sure, use hjust and vjust to change the centering. But you were
originally inserting blank spaces at the end of your axis title, and
also changing the alignment with hjust = 0.71. My point is that the
default actually does center it:

p1 <- ggplot(df1, aes(x = variable.ord, y = as.numeric(percent), fill
= value)) +
       geom_bar(stat = "identity", position = "stack") +

       coord_flip() +
       scale_y_continuous(name = "queens' behaviour during first hour

\n after introduction [%]") +

       scale_x_discrete(name = "colony state and queens elected or killed") +

       opts(legend.direction = "horizontal", legend.position = c(0.51,
0.97), legend.text = theme_text(size = 10),
             legend.title = theme_blank(), legend.background =
theme_rect(colour = 0), legend.key = theme_rect(colour = 0),
             legend.key.size = unit(c(0.6, 0.6), "lines")) +

       scale_fill_grey()

# axis titles are centered by default.
p1

## axis titles are not centered because you messed with the hjust and
vjust settings.
p1 + opts(axis.title.x = theme_text(size = 11, vjust = -0.25, hjust = 0.71),

          axis.title.y = theme_text(size = 11, hjust = 0.8, vjust =
0.24, angle = 90))

Now you may want the axis title to be centered within the plotting
area rather than the entire graphic. As far as I know this is hard,
and is something that has bugged me for awhile now. See
http://groups.google.com/group/ggplot2/browse_thread/thread/7f8a51b61af0febb/948e057f9b01971b

So in this case, for a final version of the graphic you can use hjust
by trial and error to get the positioning where you want it. There
should be no need to add extra spaces to the title.

Best,
Ista

messages.subject: Re: Heatchart with custom colours
messages.body_plain:
Hi bogu, some data to play with would be great. Something along these lines will get you there.

cars <- ggplot(mtcars, aes(y=factor(cyl), x= mpg))
cars + stat_bin(aes(fill=..count..),
geom = "tile", binwidth=3, position="identity") +
stat_bin(aes(label=..count..),
geom = "text", binwidth=3, position="identity")

Then look at geom_tile at http://had.co.nz/ggplot2/geom_tile.html and scale_fill_*. You've got different choices, look at
http://had.co.nz/ggplot2/scale_hue.html for example.

messages.subject: Is it possible to display every nth error bar?
messages.subject_clean: Is it possible to display every nth error bar?
messages.body_plain:
I'm building a line graph and adding error bars to it.  Currently, my (simplified) code looks like this:

ggplot(df,aes(time,S,color=Sex))
     +geom_point()
     +geom_errorbar(aes(x=time,ymin=S-Err,ymax=S+Err))

And everything works as expected.

The only problem is that my dependent variable (S) is sampled at about 200 values of the dependent variable (time), and having 200 error bars makes the graph unreadable.  Is there a way to just display every (say...) tenth error bar?  It seems like there should be a simple trick I'm not thinking of.

Many thanks for any thoughts you might have.
Geoff

messages.subject: geom_ribbon() with varying fill
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I'm trying to plot a ribbon that has its fill varying. So far I was
able to simulate it with geom_linerange:

geom_linerange(aes(x=ms,ymin=HC, ymax=LC, color=corelation), size=2)

so that adjacent lines stick and fill all the space. But this is not
perfect solution, because sometimes they slightly overlap, and lead to
'rough' edges.

I also thought about subdividing the x-axis domain into a few parts,
and plotting separate ribbons for them, using different colors
(basing on 'corelation' value). But this would be a dirty solution - I
would have to define new columns for each of the subdomains
(containins separate specifications for x, ymin and ymax for each of
the subdomains), and there would be still gaps in between adjacent
ribbons.

I understand the problem with geom_ribbon() not accepting varying fill
has something to do with the fact that fill is defined for discrete
points, while ribbon is continuous. But is there any other solution
around this?

Best,
Jakub

messages.subject: Convex hulls in scatter plots
messages.body_plain:
Hi everybody,

I was wondering if there is an elegant way to produce convex hulls for
several groups in scatterplots created with the ggplot2 package. I
found this post by learnr very helpful:
http://learnr.wordpress.com/2009/04/23/ggplot2-dont-try-this-with-excel/
The use of the geom_path() or geom_polygon() seem logical to
accomplish this, but the solution proposed in this blog doesn't seem
to work in my case. I have a quite large dataset and sometimes point
are connected in the way they are order in the dataset. I know several
packages who offer functions to calculate convex hulls for x and y
data (e.g. chull() ) in package grDevices). Is there some easy way to
integrate their use with ggplot ??? I guess if we can somehow select
the points from the main dataset who lie on the convex hull as
calculated by chull() or a similar functions and connect them with
lines (geom_path) or polygons (geom_polygon) shoudl do the trick.

I am a beginner in R and found ggplot quite straight forward and easy
to use, but i don't know how to do this.
Your help would be greatly appreciated.

Kenneth

messages.subject: Re: Convex hulls in scatter plots
messages.body_plain:
Hi Kenneth,

The basic idea is something like:

library(ggplot2)

df <- data.frame(x = rnorm(100), y = rnorm(100))
ggplot(df, aes(x, y)) + geom_point()

hull <- df[chull(df$x, df$y), ]
ggplot(df, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_polygon(data = hull, fill = NA, colour = "grey50")

If you have multiple groups, you'd need to use ddply or similar to
compute the convex hull for each group.

Hadley

messages.subject: Re: geom_ribbon() with varying fill
messages.body_plain:
Hi Hadley,

I am sorry, I thought this is a well-known feature/bug of ggplot2 I
was showing, this is why I provided no real example. Here it goes:

N <- 100
df <- data.frame(time=1:N, LC=rnorm(N, 70, 20), HC=rnorm(N, 20, 20),
corr=seq(-1, 0.98, 0.02))
ggplot(df, aes(x=time)) + geom_ribbon(aes(ymin=HC, ymax=LC,
fill=corr))

The above doesn't work ("Aesthetics can not vary with a ribbon")
This simulates it but is not ideal:

ggplot(df, aes(x=time)) + geom_linerange(aes(x=time, ymin=HC, ymax=LC,
color=corr), size=2)

Finally, I found a solution how to do it (thanks to James McCreight
for turning my attention to geom_polygon()!), but it needs some more
playing around:

mdf <- melt (df, id.vars=c("time", "corr"))
mdf <- mdf[order (mdf$time, mdf$variable),]
mdf <- rbind (mdf[1:(nrow (mdf) - 2),], mdf[3:nrow (mdf),])
mdf$grouping <- rep (rep (1:(N-1), each=2), 2)

messages.subject: Re: Convex hulls in scatter plots
messages.body_plain:
Hi Kenneth,

Something like this:

library(ggplot2)

df <- data.frame(x = rnorm(100), y = rnorm(100),
  z = sample(letters[1:5], 100, rep = T))
ggplot(df, aes(x, y, colour = z)) + geom_point()

find_hull <- function(df) df[chull(df$x, df$y), ]
hulls <- ddply(df, "z", find_hull)

ggplot(df, aes(x, y, colour = z)) +
 geom_point() +
 geom_polygon(data = hulls, fill = NA)

But be careful with the use of hulls.  The tend to make clusters look
more distinct than they really are (due to the gestalt of
connectedness/containedness)

df$cl <- factor(kmeans(df[c("x", "y")], 3)$cluster)
hulls <- ddply(df, "cl", find_hull)

# No obvious clusters
ggplot(df, aes(x, y, colour = cl)) +
 geom_point()

# Now clusters are really obvious!!
ggplot(df, aes(x, y, colour = cl)) +
 geom_point() +
 geom_polygon(data = hulls, fill = NA)

Hadley

messages.subject: proportional symbol map ggplot
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

we want to plot a proportional symbol map with ggplot. Symbols' area
should
have the same proportions as the scaled variable.
Hereby an example we found on
http://www.r-bloggers.com/bubble-chart-by-using-ggplot2/ . In this
example
we see the proportions of the symbols' area are different from the
proportions of the scaled variable:

crime <-
read.csv("http://datasets.flowingdata.com/crimeRatesByState2008.csv",
header=TRUE, sep="\t")
p <- ggplot(crime, aes(murder,burglary,size=population, label=state))
p <- p+geom_point(colour="red") +scale_area(to=c(1,20))
+geom_text(size=3)

Example:
proportion population Pennsylvania/Tennessee= 2.003
proportion symbols' area Pennsylvania/Tennessee= +/- 2.50

proportion population California/Florida= 2.005
proportion symbols' area California/Florida= +/-2.25

What we would like is that the proportion of the symbols' area is also
equal
to 2.0.

We see the same in the legend:
proportion population 1.6e+07 / 4.0e+06 = 4.0
proportion symbols' area 1.6e+07 / 4.0e+06= +/-5.0

Thanks in advance!

Ann Frederix
Robbie Heremans

messages.body_plain:
Hey all!

I just started using ggplot and I am blown away by the functionality!
I did figure out quite a bit already but have the following question:

I am measuring leaf senescence of 7different trees at 5 different
times (x) in scores ranging from 1 to 7 (y).
So, my factor is tree with 7 levels and 45 and 60 independent
observations per tree. Hence I have a lot of over-plotting (since the
score can only be 1 to 7). I would like to do a line plot with the

messages.subject: Re: calculating means within ggplot
messages.body_plain:
Hi:

There are basically two ways to go about this type of problem:
  (1) Let ggplot2 do the summaries.
  (2) Provide the summaries yourself and add layers to the plot using the summary data.

The latter strategy gives you more control. Here's an example based on your description.

# Manufactured data:
d <- data.frame(tree = rep(1:7, each = 50),
                score = sample(1:7, 350, replace = TRUE))

# (1) Let ggplot2 do the work:
g <- ggplot(d, aes(x = tree, y = score))
g + geom_point(position = position_jitter(width = 0.2, height = 0.2), alpha = 0.2) +
    stat_summary(fun.data = 'mean_sdl', geom = 'errorbar', width = 0.2, size = 1) +
    stat_summary(fun.y = mean, geom = 'point', size = 3, color = 'red') +
    stat_summary(fun.y = mean, geom = 'line', size = 1, color = 'red')

This 'works', but the mean_sdl() function computes means and standard deviations, not means and standard errors. I don't know offhand how, or if, mean_sdl() can produce standard errors instead of standard deviations; perhaps someone else can chime in on that point, with perhaps a different summary function.

The second approach, which I prefer in my own work, is to summarize the data prior to plotting so that I have control over what gets plotted. This also aids in the design of the graphic.

# Summary data frame, generated by the ddply() function in package plyr, which loads with ggplot2
ds <- ddply(d, 'tree', summarise, mean = mean(score),
                                   se = sd(score)/sqrt(length(score)) )

g + geom_point(position = position_jitter(width = 0.2, height = 0.2), alpha = 0.2) +
    geom_point(data = ds, aes(y = mean), size = 3, colour = 'red') +
    geom_line(data = ds, aes(y = mean), size = 1, colour = 'red') +
    geom_errorbar(data = ds, aes(y = mean, ymin = mean - se, ymax = mean + se),
                     width = 0.3, size = 1)

There are just as many lines of plot code, but in geom_errorbar() I can specify ymin and ymax in terms of standard errors computed in the summary data frame. The latter graph is meant to be consonant with your expectations; I'll let you decide whether or not they do. I jittered the points and reduced the alpha transparency so that the error bars and mean lines were emphasized, but it's merely an idea for you to consider.

HTH,
Dennis

On Tue, Mar 15, 2011 at 11:07, Rudolf Cardinal <rud...@pobox.com> wrote:

> Dear all,
>
> A quick and simple technique post, and apologies if this is obvious/already implemented somewhere else.
>
> I was trying to have ggplot2 display only left and bottom ("L"-shaped) borders, rather than a rectangle or no border, and saw on the web that this has been a problem for others. My solution (based on the ggplot2 source code in theme-elements.r) is pasted below, and is accessible directly from R using:
>
>    source("http://egret.psychol.cam.ac.uk/statistics/R/extensions/rnc_ggplot2_border_themes.r" <http://egret.psychol.cam.ac.uk/statistics/R/extensions/rnc_ggplot2_border_themes.r>)
>
> This code allows the use of one of the following ggplot2 elements:
>
>     opts( panel.border = theme_L_border() )
>
>     opts( panel.border = theme_left_border() )
>
>     opts( panel.border = theme_bottom_border() )
>
> or, to put it into a more concrete example:
>
>     library(ggplot2)
>     source("http://egret.psychol.cam.ac.uk/statistics/R/extensions/rnc_ggplot2_border_themes.r" <http://egret.psychol.cam.ac.uk/statistics/R/extensions/rnc_ggplot2_border_themes.r>)
>     df = data.frame(x=c(1,2,3),y=c(4,5,6))
>     ggplot(data=df, aes(x=x, y=y)) + geom_point() + theme_bw() + opts( panel.border = theme_L_border() )
>
>
> Note that the order can be significant; for example, if you specify the L border option and then a theme, the theme settings will override the border option, so you need to specify the theme (if any) before the border option, as above.
>
> The code is shown below.
>
> all the best,
> Rudolf.
>
>
> # Rudolf Cardinal, March 2011
> # Simple extensions to ggplot2 (v0.8.7); see http://www.psychol.cam.ac.uk/statistics/R/
>
> theme_L_border <- function(colour = "black", size = 1, linetype = 1) {
>   structure(
>     function(x = 0, y = 0, width = 1, height = 1, ...) {
>       polylineGrob(
>         x=c(x+width, x, x), y=c(y,y,y+height), ..., default.units = "npc",
>         gp=gpar(lwd=size, col=colour, lty=linetype),
>       )
>     },
>     class = "theme",
>     type = "box",
>     call = match.call()
>   )
> }
>
> theme_bottom_border <- function(colour = "black", size = 1, linetype = 1) {
>   structure(
>     function(x = 0, y = 0, width = 1, height = 1, ...) {
>       polylineGrob(
>         x=c(x, x+width), y=c(y,y), ..., default.units = "npc",
>         gp=gpar(lwd=size, col=colour, lty=linetype),
>       )
>     },
>     class = "theme",
>     type = "box",
>     call = match.call()
>   )
> }
>
> theme_left_border <- function(colour = "black", size = 1, linetype = 1) {
>   structure(
>     function(x = 0, y = 0, width = 1, height = 1, ...) {
>       polylineGrob(
>         x=c(x, x), y=c(y,y+height), ..., default.units = "npc",
>         gp=gpar(lwd=size, col=colour, lty=linetype),
>       )
>     },
>     class = "theme",
>     type = "box",
>     call = match.call()
>   )
> }
>
>

messages.subject: Re: calculating means within ggplot
messages.body_plain:
Hi Stefan,
Dennis pretty much gave you the tools for this already, unless I
missed something. The unequal length in each group is not a problem at
all. Here is Dennis' example tweeked to match you description:

d <- data.frame(date = rep(1:7, each = 50),
                score = sample(1:7, 350, replace = TRUE),
                tree = rep(1:10, 35 ))

## stat_summary can actually take any function, so we define one to
return the values we want.
se <- function(x) {
    return(c(ymin=(mean(x) - (sd(x)/sqrt(length(x)))), ymax=(mean(x) +
(sd(x)/sqrt(length(x))))))
}

g <- ggplot(d, aes(x = date, y = score))
g + stat_summary(fun.data = 'se', geom = 'errorbar', width = 0.2, size = 1) +

    stat_summary(fun.y = mean, geom = 'point', size = 3, color = 'red') +

    stat_summary(fun.y = mean, geom = 'line', size = 1, color = 'red') +
    facet_wrap(~ tree)

# Or we can do the summarizing separately.

ds <- ddply(d, .(tree, date ), summarise, mean = mean(score),
                                   se = sd(score)/sqrt(length(score)) )

g + geom_point(position = position_jitter(width = 0.2, height = 0.2),
alpha = 0.2) +
    geom_point(data = ds, aes(y = mean), size = 3, colour = 'red') +
    geom_line(data = ds, aes(y = mean), size = 1, colour = 'red') +
    geom_errorbar(data = ds, aes(y = mean, ymin = mean - se, ymax = mean + se),

                     width = 0.3, size = 1) +
    facet_wrap(~ tree )

Best,
Ista

> p+geom_point(alpha=I(1/6))+geom_smooth(size=0.5)+facet_wrap(~tree)
> +xlab('Observation date')+ylab('Leaf senescence score')+theme_bw()
> +opts(axis.text.x=theme_text(angle=90))
>
> Now, I would like to have all 7 lines (without any points) in one plot
> connected by their means over the 5 different sampling dates. When I
> can, I avoid calculating mean and standard errors; instead I really
> like boxplots since they show everything. In that case though, it
> would look a bit messy. So, I now have to get the standard errors (or
> conf.limits) that describe the mean. I usually use the doSummary()
> function in the doBy package and calculate the mean by 'score~tree
> +date' (but I checked out the ddply, which is pretty cool, too! Thanks
> for pointing it out Dennis!). But the problem is my uneven sample size
> per clone. I did calculate the SEs in excel pretty quickly and
> reimported everything into R, which is a workaround I really don't
> like.
>
> So, I was wondering if there is a way that ggplot2 does recognizes the
> length of the variables it summarizes. I agree with you Dennis that
> doing it outside ggplots2 gives you more control about what is going
> to be plotted but I can't really figure out a smart way of doing so.
>
> Thanks again guys for all the time you put into reading and answering
> all these questions!
>

>

> On Mar 14, 9:09 pm, Dennis Murphy <djmu...@gmail.com> wrote:
>> Hi:
>>
>> There are basically two ways to go about this type of problem:
>>   (1) Let ggplot2 do the summaries.
>>   (2) Provide the summaries yourself and add layers to the plot using the
>> summary data.
>>
>> The latter strategy gives you more control. Here's an example based on your
>> description.
>>
>> # Manufactured data:
>> d <- data.frame(tree = rep(1:7, each = 50),
>>                 score = sample(1:7, 350, replace = TRUE))
>>
>> # (1) Let ggplot2 do the work:
>> g <- ggplot(d, aes(x = tree, y = score))
>> g + geom_point(position = position_jitter(width = 0.2, height = 0.2), alpha
>> = 0.2) +
>>     stat_summary(fun.data = 'mean_sdl', geom = 'errorbar', width = 0.2, size
>> = 1) +
>>     stat_summary(fun.y = mean, geom = 'point', size = 3, color = 'red') +
>>     stat_summary(fun.y = mean, geom = 'line', size = 1, color = 'red')
>>
>> This 'works', but the mean_sdl() function computes means and standard
>> deviations, not means and standard errors. I don't know offhand how, or if,
>> mean_sdl() can produce standard errors instead of standard deviations;
>> perhaps someone else can chime in on that point, with perhaps a different
>> summary function.
>>
>> The second approach, which I prefer in my own work, is to summarize the data
>> prior to plotting so that I have control over what gets plotted. This also
>> aids in the design of the graphic.
>>
>> # Summary data frame, generated by the ddply() function in package plyr,
>> which loads with ggplot2
>> ds <- ddply(d, 'tree', summarise, mean = mean(score),
>>                                    se = sd(score)/sqrt(length(score)) )
>>
>> g + geom_point(position = position_jitter(width = 0.2, height = 0.2), alpha
>> = 0.2) +
>>     geom_point(data = ds, aes(y = mean), size = 3, colour = 'red') +
>>     geom_line(data = ds, aes(y = mean), size = 1, colour = 'red') +
>>     geom_errorbar(data = ds, aes(y = mean, ymin = mean - se, ymax = mean +
>> se),
>>                      width = 0.3, size = 1)
>>
>> There are just as many lines of plot code, but in geom_errorbar() I can
>> specify ymin and ymax in terms of standard errors computed in the summary
>> data frame. The latter graph is meant to be consonant with your
>> expectations; I'll let you decide whether or not they do. I jittered the
>> points and reduced the alpha transparency so that the error bars and mean
>> lines were emphasized, but it's merely an idea for you to consider.
>>
>> HTH,
>> Dennis
>>
>> On Mon, Mar 14, 2011 at 5:47 PM, Stefan
>> <stefan.schrei...@ales.ualberta.ca>wrote:

On Wed, Mar 16, 2011 at 12:07 AM, Rudolf Cardinal <rud...@pobox.com> wrote:
> Dear all,
>
> A quick and simple technique post, and apologies if this is obvious/already
> implemented somewhere else.
>
> I was trying to have ggplot2 display only left and bottom ("L"-shaped)
> borders, rather than a rectangle or no border, and saw on the web that this
> has been a problem for others. My solution (based on the ggplot2 source code
> in theme-elements.r) is pasted below, and is accessible directly from R
> using:
>
>
> source("http://egret.psychol.cam.ac.uk/statistics/R/extensions/rnc_ggplot2_border_themes.r")
>
> This code allows the use of one of the following ggplot2 elements:
>
>     opts( panel.border = theme_L_border() )
>
>     opts( panel.border = theme_left_border() )
>
>     opts( panel.border = theme_bottom_border() )
>
> or, to put it into a more concrete example:
>
>     library(ggplot2)
>
> source("http://egret.psychol.cam.ac.uk/statistics/R/extensions/rnc_ggplot2_border_themes.r")
>     df = data.frame(x=c(1,2,3),y=c(4,5,6))
>     ggplot(data=df, aes(x=x, y=y)) + geom_point() + theme_bw() + opts(
> panel.border = theme_L_border() )
>
>
> Note that the order can be significant; for example, if you specify the L
> border option and then a theme, the theme settings will override the border
> option, so you need to specify the theme (if any) before the border option,
> as above.
>
> The code is shown below.
>
> all the best,
> Rudolf.
>
>
> # Rudolf Cardinal, March 2011
> # Simple extensions to ggplot2 (v0.8.7); see
> http://www.psychol.cam.ac.uk/statistics/R/
>
> theme_L_border <- function(colour = "black", size = 1, linetype = 1) {
>   structure(
>     function(x = 0, y = 0, width = 1, height = 1, ...) {
>       polylineGrob(
>         x=c(x+width, x, x), y=c(y,y,y+height), ..., default.units = "npc",
>         gp=gpar(lwd=size, col=colour, lty=linetype),
>       )
>     },
>     class = "theme",
>     type = "box",
>     call = match.call()
>   )
> }
>
> theme_bottom_border <- function(colour = "black", size = 1, linetype = 1) {
>   structure(
>     function(x = 0, y = 0, width = 1, height = 1, ...) {
>       polylineGrob(
>         x=c(x, x+width), y=c(y,y), ..., default.units = "npc",
>         gp=gpar(lwd=size, col=colour, lty=linetype),
>       )
>     },
>     class = "theme",
>     type = "box",
>     call = match.call()
>   )
> }
>
> theme_left_border <- function(colour = "black", size = 1, linetype = 1) {
>   structure(
>     function(x = 0, y = 0, width = 1, height = 1, ...) {
>       polylineGrob(
>         x=c(x, x), y=c(y,y+height), ..., default.units = "npc",
>         gp=gpar(lwd=size, col=colour, lty=linetype),
>       )
>     },
>     class = "theme",
>     type = "box",
>     call = match.call()
>   )
> }
>

messages.subject: RE: calculating means within ggplot
messages.body_plain:
Thanks again Ista!!

I forgot to mention that I have NAs in my data as well and using different approaches I get different standard errors:
So I used your example dataset and included some NAs

require(plyr)

d <- data.frame(date = rep(1:7, each = 50),
                score = sample(1:7, 350, replace = TRUE),
                tree = rep(1:10, 35 ))

d$score <- ifelse(d$score==6,NA,d$score)

#First approach removing the NAs within the ddply function:
d1 <- ddply(d, .(tree, date ), summarise, mean = mean(score,na.rm=T),se = sd(score,na.rm=T)/sqrt(length(score)))

#Second approach removing NAs before using ddply function:
d0 <- subset(d,!is.na <http://is.na>(d$score))
d2 <- ddply(d0, .(tree, date ), summarise, mean = mean(score),se = sd(score)/sqrt(length(score)))

Now, looking at these to datasets there some standard errors that are not the same.

I assume that when removing the NAs within ddply the sqrt(length(score)) still includes the rows which have NAs.

I think in this special case it would be better to go for the second approach, or what would you suggest?

Also then (assuming all the NAs), I cannot really do the calculation within ggplot2 using the stat_summary() function?

Thanks for your help!

Stefan

-----Original Message-----
From: ista...@gmail.com on behalf of Ista Zahn
Sent: Tue 3/15/2011 8:46 AM
To: Schreiber, Stefan
Cc: ggplot2
Subject: Re: calculating means within ggplot

Hi Stefan,
Dennis pretty much gave you the tools for this already, unless I
missed something. The unequal length in each group is not a problem at
all. Here is Dennis' example tweeked to match you description:

d <- data.frame(date = rep(1:7, each = 50),
                score = sample(1:7, 350, replace = TRUE),
                tree = rep(1:10, 35 ))

## stat_summary can actually take any function, so we define one to
return the values we want.
se <- function(x) {
    return(c(ymin=(mean(x) - (sd(x)/sqrt(length(x)))), ymax=(mean(x) +
(sd(x)/sqrt(length(x))))))
}

g <- ggplot(d, aes(x = date, y = score))
g + stat_summary(fun.data = 'se', geom = 'errorbar', width = 0.2, size = 1) +
    stat_summary(fun.y = mean, geom = 'point', size = 3, color = 'red') +
    stat_summary(fun.y = mean, geom = 'line', size = 1, color = 'red') +
    facet_wrap(~ tree)

# Or we can do the summarizing separately.

ds <- ddply(d, .(tree, date ), summarise, mean = mean(score),
                                   se = sd(score)/sqrt(length(score)) )

g + geom_point(position = position_jitter(width = 0.2, height = 0.2),
alpha = 0.2) +
    geom_point(data = ds, aes(y = mean), size = 3, colour = 'red') +
    geom_line(data = ds, aes(y = mean), size = 1, colour = 'red') +
    geom_errorbar(data = ds, aes(y = mean, ymin = mean - se, ymax = mean + se),
                     width = 0.3, size = 1) +
    facet_wrap(~ tree )

Best,
Ista

messages.subject: Re: wrong data frame for stat_contour?
messages.body_plain:
Hi:

Contour plots are generally produced by constructing a grid in the x-y plane and then mapping values of z to the grid. You're basically asking for a 3D scatterplot, which is not available in ggplot2. Some alternatives are cloud() in lattice, the scatterplot3d package or perhaps rgl.

If you look at the example in geom_contour(), the original volcano object is a matrix. When melted, the row and column indices become the 'x' and 'y', forming a type of grid (similar to expand.grid() ), and the values of the matrix become the z values.
> head(volcano3d)
  X1 X2 value
1  1  1   100
2  2  1   101
3  3  1   102
4  4  1   103
5  5  1   104

I manufactured an example that is similar to what you seem to want to do and replicated your finding:

> dd <- data.frame(x = rnorm(1000), y = rpois(1000, 30), z = rnorm(1000))
> ggplot(dd, aes(x, y, z = z)) + geom_contour()

Error in if (empty(new)) return(data.frame()) :
  missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed

I also tried contourplot() in lattice and ended up with an empty plot. This indicates that your data don't conform to the structure needed for contour plots, but it does work for a 3D scatterplot:

library(lattice)
contourplot(z ~ x * y, data = dd)       # empty
cloud(z ~ x * y, data = dd)                # works

If you want to get a contour plot from ggplot2, it appears you're going to need to manufacture an appropriate rectangular grid. Typically, that means the z-values are predictions from a model with covariates x and y, but not exclusively so - e.g., a spatial lattice also generates the equivalent of a grid.

Hope that clarifies matters somewhat.

Dennis

messages.subject: Re: calculating means within ggplot
messages.body_plain:
Hi:

On Tue, Mar 15, 2011 at 12:14 PM, Schreiber, Stefan <Stefan.S...@ales.ualberta.ca> wrote:
>
> Thanks again Ista!!
>
> I forgot to mention that I have NAs in my data as well and using different approaches I get different standard errors:
> So I used your example dataset and included some NAs
>
> require(plyr)
>
> d <- data.frame(date = rep(1:7, each = 50),
>                 score = sample(1:7, 350, replace = TRUE),
>                 tree = rep(1:10, 35 ))
>
> d$score <- ifelse(d$score==6,NA,d$score)
>
> #First approach removing the NAs within the ddply function:
> d1 <- ddply(d, .(tree, date ), summarise, mean = mean(score,na.rm=T),se = sd(score,na.rm=T)/sqrt(length(score)))

Almost - you need to adjust the length as well:

d1 <- ddply(d, .(tree, date ), summarise, mean = mean(score,na.rm=T), se = sd(score,na.rm=T)/sqrt(length(score[!is.na <http://is.na>(score)])))

> #Second approach removing NAs before using ddply function:
> d0 <- subset(d,!is.na <http://is.na>(d$score))
> d2 <- ddply(d0, .(tree, date ), summarise, mean = mean(score),se = sd(score)/sqrt(length(score)))
>
> Now, looking at these to datasets there some standard errors that are not the same.
>
> I assume that when removing the NAs within ddply the sqrt(length(score)) still includes the rows which have NAs.
>
> I think in this special case it would be better to go for the second approach, or what would you suggest?
>
> Also then (assuming all the NAs), I cannot really do the calculation within ggplot2 using the stat_summary() function?

You can, but you have to use the right summary function. [Thanks for the example, Ista!] To me, one advantage of the 'create the summaries yourself' approach is that you can see in advance what you'll be plotting. There's nothing wrong with stat_summary(), but it's a black box of sorts - you have to trust that it's giving you the right answers. I prefer to control the input and the output, even if it means a few extra lines of code. If something doesn't look right, I can backtrack to find the problem easily. YMMV.

I assume that if you want to plot means + errorbars for each tree that you'll be doing so in separate panels of a faceted plot rather than a combined one. I can see plotting the mean profiles over day in a single plot - that isn't hard and overlaps are not that visually distracting - but if you intend to augment them with error bars, I predict you'll end up with a mess unless your mean profiles are well separated and your standard errors are small. With a response range of 1-7 and seven tree profiles, that doesn't seem likely...but I'm a skeptic by nature :)

Example (admittedly a bit extreme but it illustrates the point):

d <- data.frame(tree = factor(rep(c(18, 24, 32, 33, 36, 48, 52), each = 50)),
                date = rep(rep(c(1, 2, 3, 5, 8), each = 10), 7),

                score = sample(1:7, 350, replace = TRUE))

d$score[c(27, 59, 122, 205, 300)] <- NA

dsumm <- ddply(d, .(tree, date), summarise, mean = mean(score, na.rm = TRUE),
         se = sd(score,na.rm=T)/sqrt(length(score[!is.na <http://is.na>(score)])) )

g <- ggplot(dsumm, aes(x = date, y = mean, group = tree))
g + geom_point(aes(colour = tree), size = 2.5) +
    geom_line(aes(colour = tree), size = 1)

last_plot() + geom_errorbar(aes(colour = tree, ymin = mean - se, ymax = mean + se),
                    width = 0.2, size = 1)
last_plot() + facet_wrap(~ tree)

HTH,
Dennis

Hi:

Use opts(axis.text.x = theme_text(size = xx)), where xx is the desired font size.

df <- data.frame(gp = rep(c('M', 'SM'), each = 10),
                  y = rnorm(20, m = rep(c(5, 8), each = 10)) )
ggplot(df, aes(x = gp, y = y)) + geom_boxplot() +

    scale_x_discrete(breaks=c("M", "SM"), labels=c("Manejo <15 años", "Manejo >15 años"))

 last_plot() +  opts(axis.text.x = theme_text(size = 14))

HTH,
Dennis

-----Original Message-----
From: Dennis Murphy [mailto:djm...@gmail.com]
Sent: Tue 3/15/2011 6:28 PM
To: Schreiber, Stefan
Cc: ggplot2
Subject: Re: calculating means within ggplot

Hi:

On Tue, Mar 15, 2011 at 12:14 PM, Schreiber, Stefan <
Stefan.S...@ales.ualberta.ca> wrote:

>  Thanks again Ista!!
>
> I forgot to mention that I have NAs in my data as well and using different
> approaches I get different standard errors:
> So I used your example dataset and included some NAs
>
> require(plyr)
>
> d <- data.frame(date = rep(1:7, each = 50),
>                 score = sample(1:7, 350, replace = TRUE),
>                 tree = rep(1:10, 35 ))
>
> d$score <- ifelse(d$score==6,NA,d$score)
>
> #First approach removing the NAs within the ddply function:
> d1 <- ddply(d, .(tree, date ), summarise, mean = mean(score,na.rm=T),se =
> sd(score,na.rm=T)/sqrt(length(score)))
>

Almost - you need to adjust the length as well:

d1 <- ddply(d, .(tree, date ), summarise, mean = mean(score,na.rm=T), se =
sd(score,na.rm=T)/sqrt(length(score[!is.na <http://is.na>(score)])))
>
> #Second approach removing NAs before using ddply function:
> d0 <- subset(d,!is.na <http://is.na>(d$score))
> d2 <- ddply(d0, .(tree, date ), summarise, mean = mean(score),se =
> sd(score)/sqrt(length(score)))
>
> Now, looking at these to datasets there some standard errors that are not
> the same.
>
> I assume that when removing the NAs within ddply the sqrt(length(score))
> still includes the rows which have NAs.
>
> I think in this special case it would be better to go for the second
> approach, or what would you suggest?
>
> Also then (assuming all the NAs), I cannot really do the calculation within
> ggplot2 using the stat_summary() function?
>

You can, but you have to use the right summary function. [Thanks for the
example, Ista!] To me, one advantage of the 'create the summaries yourself'
approach is that you can see in advance what you'll be plotting. There's
nothing wrong with stat_summary(), but it's a black box of sorts - you have
to trust that it's giving you the right answers. I prefer to control the
input and the output, even if it means a few extra lines of code. If
something doesn't look right, I can backtrack to find the problem easily.
YMMV.

I assume that if you want to plot means + errorbars for each tree that
you'll be doing so in separate panels of a faceted plot rather than a
combined one. I can see plotting the mean profiles over day in a single plot
- that isn't hard and overlaps are not that visually distracting - but if
you intend to augment them with error bars, I predict you'll end up with a
mess unless your mean profiles are well separated and your standard errors
are small. With a response range of 1-7 and seven tree profiles, that
doesn't seem likely...but I'm a skeptic by nature :)

Example (admittedly a bit extreme but it illustrates the point):

d <- data.frame(tree = factor(rep(c(18, 24, 32, 33, 36, 48, 52), each =
50)),
                date = rep(rep(c(1, 2, 3, 5, 8), each = 10), 7),
                score = sample(1:7, 350, replace = TRUE))
d$score[c(27, 59, 122, 205, 300)] <- NA

dsumm <- ddply(d, .(tree, date), summarise, mean = mean(score, na.rm =
TRUE),
         se = sd(score,na.rm=T)/sqrt(length(score[!is.na <http://is.na>(score)])) )

g <- ggplot(dsumm, aes(x = date, y = mean, group = tree))
g + geom_point(aes(colour = tree), size = 2.5) +
    geom_line(aes(colour = tree), size = 1)

last_plot() + geom_errorbar(aes(colour = tree, ymin = mean - se, ymax = mean
+ se),
                    width = 0.2, size = 1)
last_plot() + facet_wrap(~ tree)

HTH,
Dennis

> Thanks for your help!
>
> Stefan
>

library(ggplot2)
library(maps)
data(us.cities)
big_cities <- subset(us.cities, pop > 500000)

...on top of a county-level choropleth map, like those described here:
http://blog.revolutionanalytics.com/2009/11/choropleth-challenge-result.html

library(ggplot2)
library(maps)

unemp <- read.csv("unemployment09.csv", header = F, stringsAsFactors =
F)
names(unemp) <- c("id", "state_fips", "county_fips", "name", "year",
  "?", "?", "?", "rate")
unemp$county <- tolower(gsub(" County, [A-Z]{2}", "", unemp$name))
unemp$state <- gsub("^.*([A-Z]{2}).*$", "\\1", unemp$name)

county_df <- map_data("county")
names(county_df) <- c("long", "lat", "group", "order", "state_name",
"county")
county_df$state <- state.abb[match(county_df$state_name,
tolower(state.name <http://state.name>))]

state_df <- map_data("state")

# Combine together
choropleth <- merge(county_df, unemp, by = c("state", "county"))
choropleth <- choropleth[order(choropleth$order), ]
# Discretise rate to use with Brewer colour scheme - many options here
choropleth$rate_d <- cut_number(choropleth$rate, 5)
choropleth$rate_d <- cut_interval(choropleth$rate, 5)

2), 35))

# Once you have the data in the right format, recreating the plot is
straight

ggplot(choropleth, aes(long, lat, group = group)) +
  geom_polygon(aes(fill = rate_d), colour = alpha("white", 1/2), size
= 0.2) +
  geom_polygon(data = state_df, colour = "white", fill = NA) +

I can't seem to add geom_points() to this ggplot statement, and
par(new=TRUE) doesn't seem to work either. Thanks in advance for any

Damian

messages.body_plain:
Dear Baptiste,

Good idea! I've added a theme_border(type=..., ...) function (pasted
below, and the web version of the source now has all four). The type
parameter matches your "library(gridExtra); example(borderGrob)" code.
Example use:

source("http://egret.psychol.cam.ac.uk/statistics/R/extensions/rnc_ggplot2_border_themes.r")
df = data.frame(x=c(1,2,3),y=c(4,5,6))
ggplot(data=df, aes(x=x, y=y)) + geom_point() + theme_bw() + opts(

panel.border = theme_border(type=9) )

all the best,
Rudolf.

# Rudolf Cardinal, March 2011
# Simple extensions to ggplot2 (v0.8.7); see http://www.psychol.cam.ac.uk/statistics/R/

theme_L_border<- function(colour = "black", size = 1, linetype = 1) {

   # use with e.g. "ggplot(...) + opts( panel.border=theme_L_border() ) + ..."

   structure(
     function(x = 0, y = 0, width = 1, height = 1, ...) {
       polylineGrob(
         x=c(x+width, x, x), y=c(y,y,y+height), ..., default.units = "npc",
         gp=gpar(lwd=size, col=colour, lty=linetype),
       )
     },
     class = "theme",
     type = "box",
     call = match.call()
   )
}

theme_bottom_border<- function(colour = "black", size = 1, linetype = 1) {

   # use with e.g. "ggplot(...) + opts( panel.border=theme_bottom_border() ) + ..."

   structure(
     function(x = 0, y = 0, width = 1, height = 1, ...) {
       polylineGrob(
         x=c(x, x+width), y=c(y,y), ..., default.units = "npc",
         gp=gpar(lwd=size, col=colour, lty=linetype),
       )
     },
     class = "theme",
     type = "box",
     call = match.call()
   )
}

theme_left_border<- function(colour = "black", size = 1, linetype = 1) {

   # use with e.g. "ggplot(...) + opts( panel.border=theme_left_border() ) + ..."

   structure(
     function(x = 0, y = 0, width = 1, height = 1, ...) {
       polylineGrob(
         x=c(x, x), y=c(y,y+height), ..., default.units = "npc",
         gp=gpar(lwd=size, col=colour, lty=linetype),
       )
     },
     class = "theme",
     type = "box",
     call = match.call()
   )
}

theme_border<- function(type, colour = "black", size = 1, linetype = 1) {
   # use with e.g. "ggplot(...) + opts( panel.border=theme_border(type=9) ) + ..."

   structure(
     function(x = 0, y = 0, width = 1, height = 1, ...) {

       # types from: library(gridExtra); example(borderGrob)
       # 1=none, 2=bottom, 3=right, 4=top
       # 5=left, 6=B+R, 7=T+R, 8=T+L
       # 9=B+L, 10=T+B, 11=L+R, 12=T+B+R
       # 13=T+L+R, 14=T+B+L, 15=B+L+R, 16=T+B+L+R
       xlist<- c()
       ylist<- c()
       idlist<- c()
       if (type==1) { # blank; can't pass absence of coordinates, so pass a single point and use an invisible line
         xlist<- c(x,x)
         ylist<- c(y,y)
         idlist<- c(1,1)
         linetype<- "blank"
       }
       if (type==2 || type==6 || type==9 || type==10 || type==12 || type==14 || type==15 || type==16) { # bottom
         xlist<- append(xlist, c(x, x+width))
         ylist<- append(ylist, c(y, y))
         idlist<- append(idlist, c(1,1))
       }
       if (type==4 || type==7 || type==8 || type==10 || type==12 || type==13 || type==14 || type==16) { # top
         xlist<- append(xlist, c(x, x+width))
         ylist<- append(ylist, c(y+height, y+height))
         idlist<- append(idlist, c(2,2))
       }
       if (type==5 || type==8 || type==9 || type==11 || type==13 || type==14 || type==15 || type==16) { # left
         xlist<- append(xlist, c(x, x))
         ylist<- append(ylist, c(y, y+height))
         idlist<- append(idlist, c(3,3))
       }
       if (type==3 || type==6 || type==7 || type==11 || type==12 || type==13 || type==15 || type==16) { # right
         xlist<- append(xlist, c(x+width, x+width))
         ylist<- append(ylist, c(y, y+height))
         idlist<- append(idlist, c(4,4))
       }
       polylineGrob(
         x=xlist, y=ylist, id=idlist, ..., default.units = "npc",

         gp=gpar(lwd=size, col=colour, lty=linetype),
       )
     },
     class = "theme",
     type = "box",
     call = match.call()
   )
}

messages.subject: Log Scale in a barplot with fill
messages.subject_clean: Log Scale in a barplot with fill
messages.body_plain:
Dear List,

I want to create a barplot with a log10 transformed y-scale. As long
as there is only one variable, everything goes fine:

td <- data.frame(d=c(rep("a", 100), rep("b", 1000), rep("c",
1000000)))
pl <- ggplot(td)

pl + geom_bar(mapping=aes(x=d, y=..count..)) + scale_y_log10()

This produces exactly what I would expect.

However once the dataframe contains a second variable and this
variable is mapped to "fill" strange things happen once the
scale_y_log10() is added:

td <- data.frame(d=c(rep("a", 100), rep("b", 1000), rep("c",
1000000)), l=sample(c("x","y"), 1001100, replace=T))

pl <- ggplot(td)
pl + geom_bar(mapping=aes(x=d, y=..count.., fill=l))        # Works,
but you can hardly see categories "a" and "b"
pl + geom_bar(mapping=aes(x=d, y=..count.., fill=l)) +
scale_y_log10()    # Something seems to go wrong here. The total count
of "c" appears to be somewhere near 10^11. The same thing seems to
happen to the other categories

I thought of using coord_trans instead of scale_y_log10 but it throws
an error I can't really interpret:

pl + geom_bar(mapping=aes(x=d, y=..count.., fill=l)) +
coord_trans(ytrans="log10")

Error in if (length(from) == 1 || abs(from[1] - from[2]) < 1e-06)
return(mean(to)) :
  missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed

Can anyone give me a hint on what could be my mistake here?

Thanks a lot

Sebastian
